planting.note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, or sow in fall for cool climates; New Millennium is a modern New Zealand-bred strain developed for improved vigor, sturdier branching stems, and a wider, cleaner color range than older Pacific Giant seed lines.

directions: Plant in rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun, staking tall flower spikes to protect them from wind and summer storms. New Millennium delphiniums are valued by growers for sturdier, less brittle stems than older strains and a tendency toward stronger perenniality and repeat bloom when deadheaded and cut back after the first flush. Dense spikes of large, often bicolor florets open from late spring into early summer. Delphiniums demand cool summers and decline where heat and humidity are prolonged; they excel in the Pacific Northwest, Upper Midwest, and New England. All parts are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; Pagan Purples bears richly saturated deep purple florets with a contrasting white or light bee, part of the New Zealand-bred New Millennium strain.

directions: Plant in rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun, staking stems to protect the dense flower spikes from wind and storms. Pagan Purples produces deep, velvety purple blooms on sturdy stems typical of the New Millennium strain's improved vigor and branching habit. Cut spikes back after the first bloom flush to encourage a possible secondary round of flowering. Struggles in prolonged summer heat and humidity; best in cool-summer regions. All parts are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, or sow in fall for cool climates; Percival is a long-grown white-flowered selection from the classic English Pacific Giant / Round Table delphinium strain.

directions: Plant in rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun, staking tall flower spikes against wind and summer storms. Percival bears tall, densely packed spikes of pure white, semi-double florets with a dark contrasting bee, a classic companion to the darker-flowered named selections within the same old English hybrid strain. Decline is common in zones with hot, humid summers; best performance is in cool-summer regions. All parts are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, or sow in fall for cool climates; Blue Jay is a mid-blue selection from the classic English Pacific Giant / Round Table delphinium strain, with a contrasting dark bee at the flower center.

directions: Plant in rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun, staking stems against wind and summer storms. Blue Jay bears dense, semi-double, medium-blue florets with a dark central bee, giving a cleaner, brighter blue than the deep violet tones of some other named selections in the same strain. All parts are toxic if ingested; struggles in hot, humid summer climates and performs best where summers stay cool.

common_name: White Clips Carpathian Bellflower (Compact White Cup Flowers)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or early fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light afternoon shade; White Clips is the white-flowered counterpart to the popular blue 'Blue Clips' selection.

directions: White Clips forms a compact, mounding tuft of foliage covered through early to midsummer with upward-facing, pure white, cup-shaped flowers held just above the leaves. It is an outstanding choice for the front of the border, rock gardens, and edging, with a neat habit that does not need staking. Deadhead spent flowers to prolong bloom, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring. Well-drained soil is important, especially over winter.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown stock in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Stella is a free-flowering selection of the vigorous, trailing Serbian bellflower, useful for walls, slopes, and groundcover.

directions: Stella spreads into a dense, trailing mat of small, scalloped leaves smothered from late spring through summer in starry, lavender-blue flowers. It excels cascading over walls, spilling from containers, or carpeting the ground beneath taller perennials, tolerating poor soil and some drought once established. Shear back hard after the main flush of bloom to tidy the mat and encourage repeat flowering. Can spread assertively; give it room or confine with edging where a smaller planting is wanted.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown stock in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Birch Hybrid is a long-popular, compact hybrid bellflower noted for its reliable, extended bloom and dense trailing habit.

directions: Birch Hybrid forms a low, dense mat of small foliage that cascades attractively over walls, rock crevices, and container edges, bearing abundant upward-facing, lavender-blue, star-shaped flowers over a long summer season. It is sterile and sets no seed, channeling its energy into an exceptionally long and heavy bloom period rather than setting pods. Grow in gritty, well-drained soil and give light afternoon shade in hot climates; shear lightly after flushes to encourage continued bloom.

common_name: Chettle Charm Peach-Leaved Bellflower (White Bells Edged in Blue)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown stock in spring into well-drained, average garden soil; Chettle Charm prefers cooler summers and benefits from afternoon shade and reliable moisture in hot climates, same as the species.

directions: Chettle Charm bears slender wiry stems topped with distinctive cup-shaped flowers that open nearly white with a fine, delicate pale-blue thread of color tracing the edge of each petal, a subtler and more refined take on the typical blue peach-leaved bellflower. Grow in well-drained soil with some afternoon shade in warm climates, and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor, since the species can be short-lived without periodic renewal. Deadheading spent stems often encourages a second, lighter flush of bloom.

common_name: Prichard's Variety Milky Bellflower (Deep Violet-Blue Clustered Spikes)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown stock in spring or fall in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Prichard's Variety is a compact, deep-colored selection of milky bellflower prized for its bushy, well-branched habit.

directions: Prichard's Variety forms a bushy, well-branched clump of stems topped from mid to late summer with abundant clusters of rich violet-blue, bell-shaped flowers, more compact and deeply colored than the species. It makes an excellent mid-border perennial, filling the gap between early and late-summer bloomers, and pairs well with other cottage-garden perennials. Stake lightly in exposed sites, and cut back after flowering to tidy the clump; divide every few years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Kent Belle Bellflower (Deep Violet-Blue Nodding Bells)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown stock in spring or fall in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Kent Belle is a hybrid between Campanula punctata and Campanula takesimana, combining large nodding bells with a vigorous, spreading habit.

directions: Kent Belle bears large, pendant, deep violet-blue bells held along arching stems from early to midsummer, bigger and more richly colored than either parent species. It spreads steadily by rhizome to form a substantial patch in rich, moisture-retentive soil, and is best given light shade in hot climates. Remove spent flower stems to tidy the planting, and divide congested clumps every few years to control spread and maintain vigor.

common_name: Nettle-Leaved Bellflower (Silver-Felted Foliage, Nodding Cream Bells)

planting.note: Start seed indoors or plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; nettle-leaved bellflower tolerates heat and dry soil better than many Campanula species once established.

directions: Nettle-leaved bellflower forms a mound of soft, gray-green, felted, heart-shaped foliage from which arching, one-sided flower stems rise in early to midsummer bearing a row of nodding, creamy-white, bell-shaped flowers. Notably more heat- and drought-tolerant than most bellflowers once established, it performs well in average to lean, well-drained soil and needs no staking despite its arching habit. Deadhead spent stems to tidy the plant and divide congested clumps every few years in spring.

planting.note: Sow seed in late spring or early summer of the first year for bloom the following year; chimney bellflower is historically grown as a potted specimen trained up a tall stake and traditionally overwintered in a cool, frost-free space in colder climates.

directions: Chimney bellflower sends up towering, unbranched spires densely packed with large, star-shaped, blue or white flowers in summer of its second year, historically trained as a dramatic potted specimen flanking doorways and staircases in grand gardens and conservatories. Grow in rich, well-drained soil in full sun, staking the tall flowering stem securely against wind. It behaves as a short-lived, monocarpic perennial or biennial, typically dying after flowering and best renewed from fresh seed; in borderline-hardy zones it benefits from winter protection in its first year.

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, or sow the prior fall in mild climates; Dalmatian Purple is part of the compact Dalmatian series bred to flower reliably in its first year from an early sowing, unlike traditional biennial foxglove strains.

directions: Plant in partial shade in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich soil; Dalmatian Purple produces dense, well-filled spikes of rich purple, tubular, bell-shaped flowers on compact, sturdy stems that need little to no staking, a notable improvement over taller, more open traditional foxglove strains. Its compact habit and first-year flowering (from an early sowing) make it well suited to containers and smaller borders as well as naturalized woodland-edge plantings. All parts are toxic if ingested; deadhead the central spike to encourage secondary flowering.

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, or sow the prior fall in mild climates; Dalmatian White is part of the compact Dalmatian series bred to flower reliably in its first year from an early sowing.

directions: Plant in partial shade in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich soil; Dalmatian White produces dense spikes of pure white, tubular, bell-shaped flowers on compact, sturdy stems that need little staking. Its clean white color brightens shaded borders and pairs well with the other colors in the Dalmatian series for a mixed planting. All parts are toxic if ingested; deadhead the central spike to encourage smaller secondary flower spikes.

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, or sow the prior fall in mild climates; Dalmatian Cream is part of the compact Dalmatian series bred to flower reliably in its first year from an early sowing.

directions: Plant in partial shade in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich soil; Dalmatian Cream bears dense spikes of soft cream-yellow, tubular, bell-shaped flowers lightly marked inside the throat, on compact, sturdy stems needing little staking. Its soft coloring blends easily with both pastel and jewel-toned companions in the shaded border. All parts are toxic if ingested; deadhead the central spike to encourage secondary flowering.

planting.note: Start seeds indoors in late summer for fall transplanting; Camelot White is part of the Camelot series bred for first-year flowering from seed and improved heat tolerance compared to older foxglove strains.

directions: Plant in partial shade in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic, humus-rich, consistently moist soil; Camelot White produces tall spikes densely packed with pure white, tubular, pendant flowers on the same vigorous, first-year-flowering plants as the rest of the Camelot series. Its clean white color is a classic pairing with the Camelot series' cream, lavender, and rose shades for a mixed planting. All parts of Digitalis purpurea are toxic, so wear gloves when handling and site away from children and pets.

common_name: Silver Fox Foxglove (Silvery Foliage, Cream Flowers)

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost, or sow the prior fall in mild climates; Silver Fox is grown both for its felted, silvery-gray foliage and its spikes of soft cream flowers.

directions: Plant in partial shade in well-drained, fertile, humus-rich soil; Silver Fox is valued as much for its felted, silvery-gray basal foliage, which gives garden interest even before bloom, as for its spikes of soft cream, tubular flowers in its second season. Combine with other silver-leaved and pastel-flowered plants for a soft-toned shade border. All parts are toxic if ingested; deadhead the central spike to encourage smaller secondary spikes.

planting.note: Start seed indoors or plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Carillon is a dwarf selection of the genuinely perennial yellow foxglove, notably shorter and more compact than the species.

directions: Carillon forms a tidy, low rosette of foliage topped from early to midsummer by short, dense spikes of soft pale-yellow, tubular, pendant flowers lightly marked with brown netting inside the throat, a true perennial foxglove, unlike the biennial purpurea strains, returning reliably for several years where drainage is good. Its dwarf stature suits the front of the border or rock garden where taller foxgloves would overwhelm. Deadhead spent spikes to tidy the clump, though it self-sows lightly without becoming aggressive.
